questions.stem: Given that \(\sin A=t\) and \(90° \lt A \lt 180°\), then \(\cos A\) is:
questions.hint: In the range \(90° \lt A \lt 180°\) (second quadrant), cosine is negative.

steps.explain: Use the Pythagorean identity to express \(\cos A\) in terms of \(\sin A=t\), taking the square root of both sides.
Since \(90° \lt A \lt 180°\) places \(A\) in the second quadrant, where cosine is negative, choose the negative root.

questions.stem: Explain why \(\tan\theta\) is positive in the third quadrant.
options: In the third quadrant both sine and cosine are negative, and tan is sine divided by cosine, so negative ÷ negative is positive
In the third quadrant only tangent is negative, so tan is positive
In the third quadrant sine is positive and cosine is negative, so tan is positive
Tangent is positive in every quadrant
questions.hint: Use \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) and the signs of sine and cosine in the third quadrant (both x and y are negative).

steps.explain: In the third quadrant (angles between \(180^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\)) the point on the unit circle has \(x<0\) and \(y<0\).

steps.explain: So \(\cos\theta=x<0\) and \(\sin\theta=y<0\) (both negative).
Therefore.
(A negative divided by a negative is positive.)

keyPoints.note: Sine and cosine are both negative, so their quotient is positive.

questions.stem: For the following question, you must show full working. Find the exact value of \(\tan210^{\circ}\).
questions.hint: \(210^{\circ}\) is in the 3rd quadrant (between \(180^{\circ}\) and \(270^{\circ}\)). In the 3rd quadrant only TANGENT is positive. Reference angle: \(210^{\circ}-180^{\circ}\).

steps.explain: \(210^{\circ}\) is in the 3rd quadrant: \(\sin<0\), \(\cos<0\), so \(\tan=\dfrac{\sin}{\cos}>0\) (negative ÷ negative).

steps.explain: Reference angle: \(210^{\circ}-180^{\circ}=30^{\circ}\).
Exact value of \(\tan30^{\circ}\).
Why not the others: \(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) has the wrong sign (tan is positive in the 3rd quadrant); \(\pm\sqrt{3}=\pm\tan60^{\circ}\) uses the wrong reference angle.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: If \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}\) and \(0^{\circ}\le\theta\le180^{\circ}\), find the exact value(s) of \(\cos\theta\).
questions.hint: Since \(\tan\theta>0\), decide the quadrant first. Then draw a right-angled triangle with opposite \(\sqrt{7}\) and adjacent \(4\) and find the hypotenuse by Pythagoras.

steps.explain: Quadrant: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{4}>0\) and \(\theta\) is between \(0^{\circ}\) and \(180^{\circ}\), so \(\theta\) is acute (1st quadrant; tangent is negative in the 2nd). Only ONE value of \(\cos\theta\), and it is positive.
Draw the triangle: \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}\), so opp \(=\sqrt{7}\) (red) and adj \(=4\) (green). Hypotenuse by Pythagoras.

steps.explain: Cosine \(=\dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}\).

Why not the others: \(\pm\) is wrong because \(\theta\) must be acute; \(\dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{23}}\) is \(\sin\theta\); \(\dfrac{4}{3}\) uses hyp \(=\sqrt{16-7}\) (subtracted by mistake) and is greater than 1.
So the correct choice is option A.

steps.explain: Halve both sides of \(x+y=180\).
Substitute into the denominator.
Complementary angles: \(\cos(90^{\circ}-A)=\sin A\) with \(A=\dfrac{x}{2}\).
Divide.
Why not the others: \(\tan\dfrac{x}{2}\) would need \(\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\) in the denominator; \(-1\) and 0 have no basis: the values cancel exactly.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Solve the equation \(2\cos x°=\cot x°\) for \(0\le x\le360\).
questions.hint: Write \(\cot x°=\dfrac{\cos x°}{\sin x°}\), then factorise the resulting equation — you should get two separate cases to solve.

steps.explain: Rewrite \(\cot x°\) in terms of sine and cosine, then rearrange to have zero on one side.
steps.work: \(2\cos x° = \dfrac{\cos x°}{\sin x°} \Rightarrow 2\cos x°\sin x° - \cos x° = 0\)

steps.explain: Factorise out \(\cos x°\).
Solve each factor separately: \(\cos x°=0\) gives \(x=90,270\); \(\sin x°=\tfrac12\) gives \(x=30,150\).
Combine all four solutions.

questions.stem: On the same set of axes, sketch the graphs of \(y=3\sin2x\) and \(y=\cos^2x\), for \(-180°\le x\le180°\), then state the number of solutions to \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) in this domain.

parts.stem: (i) On the same set of axes, sketch the graphs of \(y=3\sin2x\) and \(y=\cos^2x\), for \(-180°\le x\le180°\).

steps.explain: \(y=3\sin2x\) has amplitude 3 and period \(180°\) (since the angle is doubled, the period is \(360°/2\)).
steps.work: \(y=3\sin2x\): amplitude 3, period 180°, passing through the origin.

steps.explain: \(y=\cos^2x\) ranges from 0 to 1 only (since it's a square), oscillating with period \(180°\) as well (since \(\cos^2x=\tfrac12(1+\cos2x)\)).
steps.work: \(y=\cos^2x\): range \([0,1]\), period 180°, equal to 1 at \(x=0,\pm180°\) and 0 at \(x=\pm90°\).

steps.explain: Sketch both curves on the same axes over \([-180°,180°]\) — the sine curve swings from \(-3\) to \(3\) while the squared-cosine curve stays flat between 0 and 1.
steps.work: Both curves plotted on \([-180°,180°]\); note where they cross — this is used in part (ii).

parts.stem: (ii) Hence, or otherwise, state the number of solutions to the equation \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) for \(-180°\le x\le180°\).
parts.hint: Solving \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) is the same as finding where the two graphs from part (i) intersect — or factorise algebraically: write \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\) and take out the common factor \(\cos x\).

steps.explain: Solving \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) is equivalent to finding where the two graphs from part (i) intersect.
steps.work: Count the crossing points of \(y=3\sin2x\) and \(y=\cos^2x\) on \([-180°,180°]\).

steps.explain: Algebraically: substitute \(\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x\) and factorise out \(\cos x\).

\(\cos x=0\) gives 2 solutions in the domain; \(6\sin x=\cos x \Rightarrow \tan x=\tfrac16\) gives another 2 solutions (one from \(\arctan\tfrac16\approx9.5°\), one from adding \(180°\) then wrapping back into range at \(\approx-170.5°\)).
Combine all solutions found.
steps.work: \(\therefore\) there are \(4\) solutions to \(3\sin2x-\cos^2x=0\) for \(-180°\le x\le180°\).

questions.stem: If \(f(\theta)=2\sqrt3\cos\theta\tan\theta+\sqrt3\tan\theta-2\cos\theta-1\), solve \(f(\theta)=0\) for \(0^\circ\leq\theta\leq360^\circ\), by initially factorising \(f(\theta)\).
